passage: Sahil had it all on a sticky note by his hostel bed. The Wi-Fi dropped on the three nights before exams. The canteen ran out of paneer on the days fest meetings were called. The warden's scooter was parked at the admin block every time. "It's a plan," he told Dolma, his wingmate, eyes bright. "They want us distracted. Nobody else has noticed." He liked that part: the feeling of seeing what others missed. Dolma listened, then took out her own phone. "Let's test it. I'll note every Wi-Fi drop this month, exam or not." Three weeks later she showed him the list: eleven drops, only three near exams. Paneer ran out on random days. The warden's scooter was at admin almost daily. Sahil read it twice, a little deflated. "Huh. It looked so neat."

qa.q: How many Wi-Fi drops did Dolma note, and how many were near exams?
qa.a: Eleven drops, only three near exams.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel so pleased with his theory?
qa.a: The feeling of seeing what others missed; he felt special for having noticed a secret plan.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that made the "plan" testable?
qa.a: She noted every Wi-Fi drop for a month, exam or not, so the pattern could be compared with chance instead of a few hand-picked moments.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt listening to Sahil's bright-eyed theory?
qa.a: Dolma may have been doubtful but kind, choosing to test it together rather than mock it.

grounding: A hostel student strings unrelated events into a secret plan and feels special, until a wingmate tests it against a month of records.

passage:
Samir bhai,
You'll laugh, but I have to tell someone. For two weeks I've been seeing 17 everywhere. The bus I take is 17. My exam seat was 17. Our old hostel room was 17. I started thinking it meant something, like the universe was lining things up for me. Honestly, it felt amazing, like being let in on a secret.
Then I remembered your line: "What would it look like if it were just chance?" So yesterday I wrote down every number I noticed from morning to night. Forty-three numbers. Three were 17. I'd only remembered the 17s because I was hunting for them.
So, no cosmic message. Just my brain collecting hits and ignoring misses. Slightly sad, weirdly relieving. Come home soon. The bus is still 17.
Kunal

qa.q: How many numbers did Kunal write down, and how many were 17?
qa.a: Forty-three numbers, and three were 17.

qa.q: How did the 17s make Kunal feel before the test?
qa.a: Amazing, like being let in on a secret that the universe was lining up just for Kunal 😊

qa.q: What did Kunal do to test the pattern, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Wrote down every number noticed in one day, so the 17s could be compared with all the misses instead of only the hits.

qa.q: How might Samir feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Samir may be pleased and a bit amused, since Samir's own question, "What would it look like if it were just chance?", helped Kunal check.

grounding: A young adult reads a secret message into a repeated number and feels special, then tests it against chance.

passage: Tenzin, it's Nirmala's confession time. Last semester I cracked a code, or thought I did. Professor Rao tells a lot of bad jokes in thermodynamics, right? Once he joked about a pressure cooker, and the next test had a pressure cooker question. Then a joke about ice in chai, and boom, a melting problem. I felt like a genius, like I'd seen what the whole class was missing. I started writing his jokes in the margin with stars. I even told two friends to study "by the jokes". Then before the final you asked me, "How many jokes didn't turn into questions?" I went back through my notes. Thirty-one jokes. Two matched. Two! The rest were about cricket and his cat. I felt a bit silly, but mostly relieved I hadn't skipped chapters for it. I studied everything after that.

qa.q: How many jokes did Nirmala count, and how many matched test questions?
qa.a: Thirty-one jokes, and two matched.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when the first two jokes matched test questions?
qa.a: Like a genius, as if Nirmala had seen something the whole class was missing.

qa.q: Which question became the turning point, and what did Nirmala do with it?
qa.a: Tenzin's "How many jokes didn't turn into questions?" Nirmala counted every joke, saw only two matched, and went back to studying everything.

qa.q: How might the two friends told to study "by the jokes" have been affected?
qa.a: They might have skipped chapters and struggled in the final, trusting a pattern that was really chance.

grounding: A student links a professor's jokes to test questions and feels specially clever, until counting shows it was chance.

passage: I'm Vikas, and I've shared a table with Sunaina in the college library since first year. This month she has a theory. The dance club's practice room lost power on three Fridays. The new CCTV camera went up outside it. The club's faculty adviser was on leave twice. "They're planning to shut us down," she told me, tapping her notebook where she'd drawn arrows between it all. "Nobody else sees it." Her eyes were bright; she seemed almost happy to be the one who'd noticed. I pointed out that the whole east wing lost power those Fridays, and the cameras went up across campus. She waved that off. "That's what they'd want us to think." I can't tell how much she really believes it. But she's added two more arrows since.

qa.q: How many Fridays did the practice room lose power?
qa.a: Three Fridays.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's bright-eyed excitement suggest about how the theory makes her feel?
qa.a: It suggests she feels special, like the only one clever enough to see a hidden plan.

qa.q: How could Sunaina test her theory instead of adding arrows?
qa.a: She could check whether other rooms lost power or got cameras too, and ask what she'd expect to see if it were all chance.

qa.q: How might the dance club's faculty adviser feel if they heard the theory?
qa.a: The adviser might be surprised or a little hurt to be cast as part of a plot for simply taking leave.

grounding: A classmate observes a young adult link unrelated events into a secret plan, pleased to have noticed it.

passage:
Monday. Elizabeth, twenty, was walking to her hostel in Kochi when the song her grandmother used to hum came on shuffle, just as she thought of her. She stopped under a streetlight, goosebumps rising.
Thursday. It had happened four more times. Elizabeth wrote each one in a notebook with the time. "It's a sign," she told Anjali at lunch, a little breathless. "Like she's telling me something. Nobody else would even notice."
Sunday. Anjali sat with her on the hostel steps. "Can I ask? How many times did the song play when you weren't thinking of her?" Elizabeth started to answer and stopped. She hadn't written those down. "And how often do you think of her?" "All the time," Elizabeth admitted. She looked at her notebook, and for the first time it seemed a bit thin.

qa.q: Where was Elizabeth walking when the song first played?
qa.a: To her hostel in Kochi.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she called it a sign?
qa.a: She felt moved and special, as if she alone had noticed a message meant for her.

qa.q: What question could help Elizabeth test the pattern, and why?
qa.a: Counting the times the song played when she wasn't thinking of her grandmother, since a real pattern should hold up against chance.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel asking questions about something so personal?
qa.a: Anjali probably feels careful and caring, wanting to help without hurting Elizabeth's feelings about her grandmother.

grounding: A young adult reads a secret meaning into coincidences and feels special, until a friend suggests testing it.
